claims.claim: SAWS operates a national weather radar network (number, sites, band, status issues incl. Durban radar outage Oct 2017 and radars offline 2020-2026).
claims.verified_wording: According to its Early Warnings for All roadmap (2025-2029), the South African Weather Service operates 11 weather radar systems (10 S-band and 1 C-band). Ten Gematronik METEOR 600S S-band radars, one of them dual-polarised at Bethlehem, were installed in 2010-2012. SAWS told the media that its Durban radar was not working because of a system breakdown during the October 2017 KwaZulu-Natal storms. SAWS's own performance reports show that its Tier 1 radars were available only 73% (2020/21), 73.83% (2021/22), 52.23% (2022/23) and 44.25% (2023/24, unaudited) of the time. Availability recovered to 80% in 2024/25, but that year the Irene and Ermelo sites had unstable power and the Irene and Polokwane sites were hit by vandalism and theft. SAWS announced that the Durban radar would be decommissioned from 15 September 2026, with a replacement due to be commissioned by 20 October 2026.

details.radar_count_history: Pre-2009: eleven Enterprise C-band radars plus one EEC S-band at Skukuza. The 2010-2012 upgrade bought 10 METEOR 600S S-band (1 dual-pol) and 2 mobile METEOR 50DX X-band radars. A 2017 SAWS abstract gives a network total of 14 radars; a 2015 AMS abstract says 16. The totals differ by date and by whether mobile/research units are counted.

claims.claim: SAWS receives EUMETSAT Meteosat geostationary satellite data covering Africa (MSG / MTG); which satellites, imagery frequency.
claims.verified_wording: EUMETSAT's Meteosat satellites cover all of Africa. Meteosat-12, the first Meteosat Third Generation imager, launched on 13 December 2022 and entered operational service on 4 December 2024. Since June 2025 it has been EUMETSAT's prime geostationary satellite for Europe and Africa, scanning the full Earth disc every 10 minutes. The older Meteosat Second Generation satellite Meteosat-10 now acts as its backup. A 2014 study states that SAWS has access to Meteosat Second Generation data. We did not find a primary source confirming that SAWS operationally receives MTG data today.

claims.claim: SAWS operates the South African Lightning Detection Network (SALDN) — number of sensors, detection efficiency.
claims.verified_wording: SAWS has operated a Vaisala lightning detection network since 2005, and it became fully operational in 2006. The number of sensors has grown from 19 at installation to 24-25 in the early 2020s. SAWS's 2025-2029 Early Warnings for All roadmap lists 26 sensors. Vaisala predicted a flash detection efficiency of 90%. A peer-reviewed study over Johannesburg measured 84.9% for flashes and 69.1% for strokes.

claims.claim: SAWS runs NWP via the Unified Model (UK Met Office partnership) — resolution 4.4 km / 1.5 km (SA4/SA1.5).
claims.verified_wording: SAWS runs a local configuration of the UK Met Office Unified Model at 4.4 km grid spacing over southern Africa and 1.5 km over South Africa. The model is updated four times a day, and the 00 UTC run of the 4.4 km model forecasts up to 72 hours ahead. Its initial and boundary conditions come from the Met Office's global model, which runs at 10 km.

claims.claim: South African Flash Flood Guidance System (SAFFG / SARFFG) — part of WMO FFGS with US Hydrologic Research Center; coverage.
claims.verified_wording: There are two separate systems. The Southern Africa Region Flash Flood Guidance system (SARFFG) is a regional system hosted by SAWS as the WMO Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre in Pretoria. It was built with the US Hydrologic Research Center (HRC), and a 2016 HRC presentation lists it as covering 10 countries. Separately, HRC implemented a national South Africa Flash Flood Guidance (SAFFG) system for SAWS from August 2017. SAFFG covers flash-flood-prone areas served by the SAWS regional forecast offices in Pretoria, Durban, Port Elizabeth and Cape Town, not the whole country.

claims.claim: SAWS impact-based warning system: colour (Yellow/Orange/Red) x levels 1-10, developed with NDMC; introduced ~2019.
claims.verified_wording: SAWS issues impact-based severe weather warnings that combine a colour (yellow, orange or red) with a level from 1 to 10. Both are set by combining how severe the expected impact is with how likely it is. SAWS says it developed the system in partnership with the National Disaster Management Centre. The date is wrong: the system began issuing public warnings in October 2020, not around 2019. It followed pilot phases with disaster managers, and SAWS's own roadmap dates its adoption of impact-based forecasting to 2017.

claims.claim: GloFAS (Copernicus) and GDACS coverage of South Africa.
claims.verified_wording: The Copernicus Global Flood Awareness System (GloFAS) is global, so it includes South African rivers. Its reanalysis produces daily discharge maps at about 5 km (0.05 degree) resolution. GDACS lists South African flood events with GloFAS as the source. They include Orange alerts for 9-11 April 2022, 9-14 June 2025, and 19 January 2026, the last covering Mozambique, South Africa and Zimbabwe. GDACS flood entries include recorded impacts such as deaths and displacement, so they partly document events after they happen and are not only advance warnings.

claims.claim: National early-warning dissemination channels: NDMC alert portal, SAWS app, cell broadcast status (ICASA), EW4All South Africa roadmap.
claims.verified_wording: South Africa's Early Warnings for All roadmap (2025-2029) was launched by CoGTA Minister Velenkosini Hlabisa on 13 October 2025 and needs an estimated $60m (about R1 billion). The roadmap acknowledges that cell broadcast and location-based SMS alerts 'might be in place' on mobile networks but are not activated for early warning. Activating them is a planned action for the communications department, ICASA and the NDMC. SAWS sends warnings through its website, social media, print and TV, more than 140 radio stations, and its WeatherSmart app, which was developed by AfriGIS. The NDMC has a directorate for early-warning platforms, but we found no public NDMC alert-subscription portal beyond a 'Receive Early Warning' contact link. We found no ICASA regulation that mandates cell broadcast alerts.

claims.claim: Count of SAWS warnings issued per year; official statements that forecasts for April 2022 KZN, June 2025 Mthatha and Jan 2026 Limpopo were accurate/timely.
claims.verified_wording: We could not find a published annual count of SAWS warnings. On the three floods: (a) April 2022, KwaZulu-Natal: SAWS said its impact-based warnings were issued in a timely manner, but that the extreme rainfall 'exceeded even the expectations of the southern African meteorological community'. It issued a Level 5 warning at 4pm on 11 April, raised it to Level 8 at 8pm, and then to Orange Level 9. (b) June 2025, Mthatha: the WMO's State of the Climate in Africa 2025 report, as reported by the Daily Dispatch, credits SAWS with a first warning statement on 5 June, five days before the floods, and an escalation to Orange Level 9 for OR Tambo district on 10 June. (c) January 2026, Limpopo: SAWS issued a rare Red Level 10 warning for Limpopo and Mpumalanga on 15 January 2026. By then, 19 people had already died in the preceding week. A University of Limpopo researcher concluded that the deaths were due to poor preparedness rather than a failure of the forecast.

Current SAWS figure is 11 radars (10 S-band, 1 C-band; EW4All Roadmap 2025), so some 2014 C-band/X-band entries are probably retired; which C-band radar remains is not stated. No official SAWS radar coordinate list found; only Irene has published coordinates, all others null. weathersa.co.za is a JS app with a certificate error, so SAWS pages were read via Wayback copies (URLs given). The EW4All roadmap PDF returned 404 live on 2026-09-25 and was read from the 26 Apr 2026 Wayback copy. The SAWS 2023/24 and 2024/25 annual reports were not retrievable (404/403), so annual warning counts could not be checked. The Fensham et al. 2023 quote is from the indexed abstract and should be checked against the article. The Durban 2017 outage and the Mthatha WMO praise come from media reports of SAWS/WMO statements, not primary documents. The '~2019' introduction date for impact-based warnings is not supported: public launch October 2020 (Met Office), with SAWS dating IBF to 2017 (pilot).
